messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 68

She is a 54-year-old European woman who has worked most of her adult life as a chef, a role that once felt steady and familiar to her. Before the assault, she describes her days as demanding but satisfying: long shifts, the sharp heat of the kitchen, the rhythm of knives on cutting boards, the pressure of timing and precision. She and her husband have been married for many years, and her work has always been one of the places where she feels competent and useful. She takes pride in feeding people well and in being able to keep a busy kitchen moving.

The assault happens one evening after work, when she is alone and not expecting anything to go wrong. She does not dwell on the details in the same way each time she tells it; what stays with her most is the suddenness of it, the immediate sense that she is trapped and cannot predict what will happen next. In the moment, she experiences a kind of freezing terror. Her body feels like it belongs to someone else. She remembers the sounds around her, the harshness of a voice, the sensation of being overpowered, and the sickening realization that she is not able to stop it. Afterward, everything feels unreal and painfully vivid at the same time. She goes home in shock, trying to function, trying to appear composed, but inside she feels scattered and contaminated by what happened.

In the days that follow, she assumes she will settle back into herself, but instead she begins to feel as though the assault is continuing in fragments. She startsle-starts easily at sudden noises, especially when something bangs in the kitchen or when someone comes up behind her without warning. Sleep becomes difficult. When she does fall asleep, she wakes abruptly, drenched in sweat, with her heart racing and her mind still locked in the scene. She tries not to think about the assault, but images and body memories intrude when she least expects them: while chopping vegetables, while locking the back door, while hearing footsteps in a hallway. She finds herself scanning rooms automatically, noting exits, checking who is nearby, and sitting with her back to walls whenever she can.

At work, the kitchen that once felt like a place of mastery becomes unpredictable and tense. The clatter of metal pans, raised voices, and fast movement around her can trigger a wave of panic that she works hard to hide. She keeps going because she feels responsible for her team, but she notices that she is more irritable and less patient than before. Small mistakes, once easily corrected, now feel intolerable. On some days she becomes tearful in the prep room for reasons she cannot fully explain. On other days she feels numb, moving through her tasks without much sense of being present. She has moments when she wonders if she is failing at the very work that has always defined her.

At home, her husband notices that she is more guarded and less spontaneous. She loves him, but even in familiar intimacy she can feel her body tense, bracing for something she cannot name. She withdraws from social gatherings and declines invitations she would once have accepted without hesitation. She tells herself she is simply tired, but the truth is that being around people now feels effortful and exposed. She avoids walking alone after dark and becomes uneasy in parking lots, stairwells, and other spaces where she cannot see everything at once. She begins planning her days around safety without fully admitting that fear is shaping so many of her choices.

As the months pass, she becomes increasingly frustrated with herself. She knows the assault is over, but her body does not seem to have received the message. She feels ashamed of how much energy it takes to get through ordinary life. She misses the version of herself who could move through a crowded kitchen with confidence, laugh easily with coworkers, and come home without first checking every lock in the house. Now she lives with a constant sense of alertness, as if danger is still nearby and she must remain ready. Even on quieter days, there is a tightness in her chest and a sense that she is waiting for the next bad thing to happen.

By the time she comes to therapy, she has been carrying this burden for a long time. She speaks about the assault in a careful, controlled way, but the emotion is close to the surface. She wants to feel safe in her own body again. She wants to cook without fear, sleep without jolting awake, and move through the world without constantly bracing herself.
